| [LIT-118](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-118.md) v2 | A Pragmatist Theory of Evidence | Reiss (2015), DOI-10.1086/681643. Reiss proposes an "eliminativist hypothetico-contextualist" (EHC) theory of evidence for type-level causal claims in biomedical and social science. Support comes in two kinds: direct support (patterns we are "entitled to expect" if h is true) and indirect support (patterns incompatible with relevant alternatives). Warrant is graded by which alternatives have been eliminated, on four grades from "weak warrant" to "proof". Where to stop probing is set by context, meaning background knowledge, a default entitlement to other scientists' claims, and cost-benefit values. On this account there is no gold standard: RCTs are good only because they eliminate many alternatives at once. The 1950s smoking–lung cancer case illustrates the theory; it does not test it. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-197](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-197.md)); worth reading as the clearest short statement of an eliminativist, anti-hierarchy account of evidence that works for observational science, and of how values and trust set stopping rules. | [LIT-139](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-139.md) v2 | Inductive Risk and Values in Science | Douglas (2000), DOI-10.1086/392855. Hempel's "inductive risk" (the chance of wrongly accepting or rejecting a hypothesis) arises at three internal stages of science: choosing a methodology such as a significance level, characterising data, and interpreting results. Wherever the non-epistemic consequences of error can be foreseen, weighing them requires non-epistemic values. Douglas shows this on dioxin cancer studies. Three pathologist panels (1978, 1980, 1990) scored the same Kociba rat-liver slides differently (e.g. 34/50, 33/47, 18/50 tumours at 100 ng/kg/day). Choosing between threshold and no-threshold readings of the same data has meant regulatory limits about 100× apart. Values enter only indirectly, through the consequences of error, never as evidence that a claim is true. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-145](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-145.md)); worth reading as the canonical, compact statement of the modern inductive-risk argument. It is carefully scoped, with an explicit direct/indirect distinction and exemptions for negligible uncertainty and consequence-free research, and it is well illustrated. Its normative premise, that scientists bear moral responsibility for foreseeable consequences of error, is explicitly left unargued (§2, p. 563). |

| [LIT-161](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-161.md) v2 | Why Replication Is Overrated | Feest (2019), DOI-10.1086/705451. Every experiment and every replication rests on individuation judgments about what is being manipulated and measured ("conceptual scope"). So direct replication can at most help rule out random error, and "perhaps" establish that some effect exists but not which effect, while conceptual replication begs the question by presupposing that two operationalisations individuate the same effect. What productive research actually does, as in the Mozart-effect debate, is probe systematic errors, which is better called exploration than replication. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-196](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-196.md)); worth reading as a short, clearly argued statement of why replication cannot settle "what effect?" questions, built on one worked case (the Mozart effect). | [LIT-162](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-162.md) v2 | Is Unsupervised Clustering Somehow Truer? | Søgaard (2024), DOI-10.1007/s11023-024-09699-5. Søgaard rebuts two arguments that unsupervised clustering is epistemically superior to supervised classification. The No-Bias Argument fails because clustering is also sensitive to sample bias (a toy example moves the boundary from x = 7 to x = 6), and it is more sensitive to representation bias. The Simplicity-Truth Argument fails because clustering is also function estimation and overfits in the same way (Hansen & Larsen 1996). From the fact that every clustering hypothesis is in a supervised classifier's hypothesis class, he concludes that supervised classification is "at least as justified", but that positive step is under-argued. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-108](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-108.md)); worth reading as a short corrective to Rochefort-Maranda & Liu's claim that unsupervised clustering cannot overfit and to "no-bias" readings of Watson. | [LIT-175](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-175.md) v2 | Evidence in Medicine and Evidence-Based Medicine | Worrall (2007), DOI-10.1111/j.1747-9991.2007.00106.x. Worrall argues that the EBM evidence hierarchy has no sound general rationale for giving randomisation extra epistemic weight, even though it lets high-quality RCTs "trump any number of observational studies". He examines five standard arguments. Four fail: (a) Fisher's significance-test logic, (b) control of unknown confounders, (d) that observational studies "exaggerate" effects, and (e) probabilistic causality. The fifth, (c) selection bias, is a "cast-iron argument", but it supports only taking allocation out of the clinicians' hands, and randomisation is one way to do that. What matters is balance on plausible confounders, a placebo or active control and blinding. Whether balance comes from randomising or from matching "seems epistemically unimportant", and historically controlled trials can give strong evidence for large effects. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-126](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-126.md)); worth reading as the fullest single statement of the philosophical case against the special epistemic standing of randomisation. It is clearly argued and well documented, and it explicitly concedes the selection-bias argument. It is a partisan position piece, and its defenders-of-randomisation opponents (Pocock, Elbourne, Papineau) are summarised, not engaged at length. |

| [LIT-187](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-187.md) v3 | On the Philosophy of Unsupervised Learning | Watson (2023), DOI-10.1007/s13347-023-00635-6. Watson argues that clustering, abstraction and generative modelling each come with an epistemic thesis (EC, EA, EG — we identify natural kinds, essential properties and unrealized possibilities via such algorithms or something like them), which he accepts. Each also comes with an ontological thesis (OC, OA, OG — these just *are* what the algorithms ought to find under ideal conditions), which he rejects because nothing guarantees they are effectively computable. He adds a pragmatic, context-relative view of natural kinds, and closes with the claim that unsupervised outputs are neither "objective" nor vacuous. They should be validated by error-statistical means: resampling stability, generalization of clusters to held-out data, out-of-sample likelihood, and train-on-synthetic scores. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-172](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-172.md)); worth reading as the most systematic philosophical treatment of unsupervised learning as a family, and as the target of Søgaard's reply. Its headline claims ("perhaps the most fundamental branch of all AI") are argued more thinly than its E/O structure. |
| [LIT-189](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-189.md) v2 | Philosophy of Open Science | Leonelli (2023), DOI-10.1017/9781009416368. Leonelli argues that mainstream, institutional Open Science treats openness as the unlimited, digital sharing of research objects, a transparency-first ordering running transparency → quality (reproducibility) → inclusion. This rests on an object-oriented, "resourcist" epistemology of science. Four implementation cases (GISAID COVID data, open-source software stigma, crop-data linkage, the reproducibility "crisis") show it can narrow epistemic diversity and entrench epistemic injustice, which lowers reliability. She proposes instead "openness as judicious connection", grounded in a process-oriented view of research as the cultivation of "active knowledge". Her Figure 2 inverts the ordering to start from inclusion, and sharing becomes "neither a necessary starting point nor a sufficient condition" for reliable OS (p. 8). | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-098](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-098.md)); worth reading as a clear, openly normative philosophical reframing of Open Science by someone who took part in the policy process, and as a compact bridge between social epistemology (epistemic injustice, pluralism) and data practice. | [LIT-213](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-213.md) v2 | Rigour versus the need for evidential diversity | Cartwright (2021), DOI-10.1007/s11229-021-03368-1. Cartwright offers a characterisation of "rigour": a method is rigorous when a valid argument shows its results are evidence for the conclusion and its premises are well established or secured by design. On that definition even well-run RCTs often fail to rigorously establish a study-population ATE, because orthogonality holds only at assignment and the potential-outcomes premise carries heavy metaphysics, and they seldom answer singular questions. Her alternative is a causal-process-tracing theory of change (pToC) with five elements (steps, causal principles, support factors, derailers, safeguards). It catalogues the diverse and mostly non-rigorous evidence that singular causal predictions need. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-161](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-161.md)); worth reading as a compact, citable statement of the "rigour is overvalued, evidence the causal process" position. The pToC template is concrete, but the paper openly offers no method for weighing the evidence it catalogues. |
| [LIT-216](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-216.md) v2 | The Weirdness of the World | Schwitzgebel (2024), DOI-10.1515/9780691239309. The book's thesis is that every viable theory of how consciousness fits into the cosmos, and of the cosmos's basic structure, is both "bizarre" (contrary to common sense) and "dubious" (not rationally compelling). So "something that seems almost too crazy to believe must be true" (p. 4), and credence should be spread across the bizarre options. Examples of those options are that the United States is conscious (if materialism is true), that we are sims or Boltzmann brains (a 0.1–1% credence), that space is transcendentally ideal, that almost every act causes almost every future event, and that there is no fact about snail consciousness. Its only positive empirical results are three self-experiments against solipsism (for example, 17 of 19 decisive chess games lost, p < .001). Everything else is informal argument. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-188.md)); Worth reading as the one place Schwitzgebel's separately published arguments are joined into a single case: US consciousness, crazyism, 1% skepticism, Kant meets cyberpunk, the garden snail, and the Full Rights Dilemma for AI. Chapter 3, the Universal Bizarreness and Dubiety argument, is the load-bearing contribution. Its individual chapters are informal arguments, and the manuscript that can be reached is not the published text. The published book reorders the chapters, moves the objections appendix to the end and updates the AI chapter. |
